title: Do Consumers Respond to Marginal or Average Price? Evidence from Nonlinear Electricity Pricing
research_question: When facing nonlinear price schedules with multiple marginal prices for the same good, do consumers actually base their consumption decisions on the marginal price, the expected marginal price, or the average price? How does the answer to this question affect whether nonlinear pricing achieves its stated goal of reducing consumption, and what are its welfare consequences?
data_description: The study uses confidential household-level monthly residential electricity billing records obtained from Southern California Edison (SCE) and San Diego Gas & Electric (SDG&E) covering January 1999 through December 2007. Each monthly observation includes the customer's account ID, premise ID, billing start and end dates, monthly kWh consumption, monthly bill amount, tariff type, climate zone, and nine-digit zip code. The main analytic sample focuses on households on the standard residential tariff residing in six Orange County cities that straddle the two utilities' service territory boundary, restricted to customers at the same premise throughout the period (40,729 households; roughly 3.75 million household-month observations). Nine-digit zip codes are matched to 2000 US Census block group data to obtain demographic and housing characteristics (income, home value, rent, household size, education, race, employment, etc.).
institutional_context: California residential electricity customers cannot choose their retail provider; service is determined by address. In most of Orange County, SCE serves the north and SDG&E serves the south, with a territory boundary established in the 1940s that, unusually, runs through the interior of six cities (Laguna Beach, Laguna Niguel, Aliso Viejo, Laguna Hills, Mission Viejo, Coto de Caza) rather than along city limits. Both utilities use increasing block (tiered) pricing tied to a climate-region baseline of roughly 10 kWh/day, but they set tariffs independently subject to California Public Utility Commission approval, reflecting differences in generation portfolios, distribution costs, and legacy costs from the 2000–2001 California electricity crisis. As a result, neighboring households in the same city face substantially different nonlinear tariffs, and the relative prices between the two utilities shifted repeatedly over 1999–2007, including the 2000 crisis price spike for SDG&E and the 2001 introduction of five-tier schedules. All households share the same natural gas provider.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: RDD — treatment = households facing higher marginal prices, control = households facing lower marginal prices; shock/instrument/cutoff = block pricing thresholds

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The study finds that consumers respond more to average prices rather than marginal prices when making electricity consumption decisions.
